utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask the Prosecution for the appearances in the new year now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution appear Mr. Daryl Mundis, Ms. Tecla Benjamin, Ms. Kimberly Fleming as the case manager, and I, Ekkehard Withopf. And I would like to use this opportunity to introduce Ms. Tecla Benjamin as a new trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic is represented by Edina Residovic and co-counsel Stephane Bourgon, and legal assistant, Ms. Milanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Mr. Kubura is represented by Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Mr. Rodney Dixon, and Mr. Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we're starting this session in this new year. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present: The Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused. We are going to proceed by hearing a witness, but before we call the witness in, I would like to take stock, examine a few pending motions, and examine our schedule. As you know, the Prosecution has submitted to us and to the Defence a provisional schedule for the week of the 12th to the 16th of January and from the 19th to the 23rd of January and from the 26th to the 30th of January. They have provided a list of witnesses. You may note that in this new list, dated the 12th of January, 2004, the 26th of January isn't scheduled for General Reinhold. That has been postponed until a later date. As far as the Prosecution's motion to modify its list of witnesses and it exhibits, as far as this motion is concerned, the Defence answered on the 18th of December and we will soon render our decision with regard to this motion. But we should point out that the Defence in its brief mentioned certain elements and also addressed the question of a military expert for the Prosecution, although it didn't give a final opinion on the so-called -- on the hearing mentioned. I'll return to that later. So we'll render our decision soon with regard to this motion. We have also been seized during the court recess and we have also been provided by a motion from the Defence concerning the cross-examination and Rule 90(H) and its scope. This motion is dated the 17th of December, and the Prosecution has provided us with its response. It did so on the 5th of January. With regard to this request, we will also soon render our decision. And I would also like to remind you that the Prosecution wanted an extension of the time limit to respond to the motion mentioned. The Prosecution's response was filed on the 6th -- on the 5th of January. We were also forwarded a motion to exclude the testimony of witnesses from other cases. As you know this issue has already been a matter of debate before this Trial Chamber. The Defence, in a request dated the 19th of December, 2003 requested that the Trial Chamber rule on this issue, and the Prosecution responded on the 9th of January, and the question that arises is to know whether the Defence stands by its request to the extent that the Prosecution has admitted that the Defence has the right to make such a request. So there are two solutions: Either you make no comments and we will render our decision and say that your request is no longer relevant, given the Prosecution's position; or you will file a new motion with the Trial Chamber and saying that your request of the 19th of December, 2003 has been dismissed. I don't know what the Defence's position is with regard to this matter, but I should point out that in a document provided by the Prosecution, the Prosecution pointed out that the new version of General Reinhold, there won't be any prior statements with regard to this, and that there won't be any questions raised with regard to this matter. So very briefly, could the Defence tell us whether it has a new position today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we received the Prosecution's document with regard to this matter, and on the 12th of January we responded to the question that you have put to us today. Very briefly, we have accepted the Prosecution's position with regard to the fact that they won't be using the testimony of the accused in the Blaskic case, so that all the segments from experts reports will be annulled and they will not refer to these -- to this testimony. We also agree with the fact that - and this is something the Prosecution pointed out - it's too early to decide today whether this testimony could be used, if the accused decides to testify. Since we have provided a written response to this matter, I think that the Trial Chamber will be in a position to render an appropriate decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So as far as I have understood, you have filed a written response to the Prosecution's position. I haven't received this response yet. But we will decide on the matter. We have also been seized of -- asked to provide protective measures for two witnesses, one who should be coming in the course of this month and the second one, who should be appearing in February. The Defence has also submitted a brief to us with regard to this matter. And we will make a ruling. I would like to point out that you also requested the disclosure of documents pertaining to the Blaskic case, and all this is pending before the Appeals Chamber. It is thus necessary to wait for the Appeals Chamber decision to see whether these requests will all be granted. As everyone has been working over the holiday period, the Prosecution has also filed a motion concerning Rule 92 bis, which concerns witnesses who could be called before this jurisdiction, within the scope of Rule 92 bis. The Prosecution has therefore provided us with this list of witnesses, and the Defence filed its response and stated that it was opposed to the list for Witnesses 15, 21, 131, and 82. So we will be deciding on the matter as soon as possible. But I should point out that it is not a matter of urgency, but we will soon address this matter, since we have all the elements that are relevant to the issue. And finally, the Prosecution has filed with us and also provided a corrigendum, because they noted that there were footnotes and references that contained errors, and this document provides corrections to the errors that were observed. So you've had the Prosecution's document; you received it on the 19th of December. There are amendments -- there are changes that were made in footnotes which concern the references. So I have briefly gone over the pending motions. I don't think I have forgotten to mention any elements. These motions will therefore be examined. Does the Defence have any comments to make? But I should point out that with regard to the archives of the European Union, I don't have any elements. Perhaps the Defence has received other elements since that time. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would first of all like to say that in your decision, you have bound the Defence to express its position by the 12th of January with regard to the findings of the military expert too. In accordance with your decision, we have also provided a written response today, and this is one of the requests that is outstanding, and we discussed this before court recess. As far as the documents are concerned, the European monitors's documents, I would briefly like to inform you about the measures that the Defence has so far taken -- has so far taken in order to examine these documents, since the Defence considers that this is of extreme importance for the defence of our clients and also for the proceedings. According to your decision, dated the 15th of December, we took certain measures on several occasions. We contacted the general secretary of the Council of Europe and the Mission of the European Observers, the European Observers Mission in Sarajevo, in order to discuss with them how it might be possible to gain access to these archives. On the 5th of January, we were informed by the European Monitors Mission in Sarajevo that they were not at all familiar with the decisions of the Trial Chamber, and at their request we provided them with a copy by fax, and with regard to this response we also contacted the office of Mr. Solana, the general secretary, in order to talk to those responsible about this issue. Mr. Miller [phoen] was absent, but we were also informed that he would be phoning us at a later date. To date we haven't received a response from Mr. Miller, but we have had contacts with other people in positions of responsibility. On the 6th of January, we contacted the Registry in order to make sure that the decision of the Trial Chamber was forwarded to the general secretary, Mr. Solana, in accordance with the Trial Chamber's order, and on the 7th of January, the Registry informed us that that decision had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been forwarded on the 23rd of December, 2003. We continued to contact all those responsible in an attempt to obtain a decision as soon as possible with regard to access to the archives, in order to respect your decision that access to the archives -- that this matter should be completed by the 30th of January of this year. This morning, when speaking to a responsible person in Brussels, we were informed that they had received the decision only yesterday and that we didn't have to contact the ambassador in Sarajevo. We were told that we would soon be receiving a response. We were informed that the Trial Chamber's decision was that we should have access to the archives by the end of January. We're going to continue on insisting on this contact, but the situation today is as stated in the written response that we received from Brussels this morning. Thank you. With regard to this issue, Mr. President, if we are granted the possibility of examining the archives, for the sake of examining all the documents rapidly and efficiently in the archives - and there are tens or hundreds of thousands of documents in the archives - for this reason, we would probably request the Trial Chamber pause -- have a break in the proceedings for two days so that the teams could go and examine these documents as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Concerning the suspension of the proceedings for a two-day period, I have noted -- I have observed that in the schedule there is a day when there is no hearing scheduled because of technical maintenance in the courtroom. So we already have one day that could be used. But since there are three of you - or in fact, there are six lawyers for the Defence - it's sufficient for two -- that two representatives of the Defence go to examine the archives and the others can stay here. But as you know, in our decision, we have a deadline for a response from the European Union. But if there is no response, we will go into the following stage, which will be a matter of issuing an order, a binding order. So I think that this should be dealt with as rapidly as possible. The Trial Chamber thanks you for all your attempts to find a solution as rapidly as possible to this matter and so that you may be granted access to these documents, enabling the case to proceed efficiently, both for the Prosecution, the Defence, and naturally for the Tribunal. Is there anything that the Prosecution would like to comment on before we call the first witness in?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Very briefly. Two observations: The first concerns the Defence response to the Prosecution motion to amend its list of witnesses and exhibits. The Prosecution has meanwhile provided Defence counsel with a complete list of all documents given to the military expert, and the Prosecution has also provided Defence counsel with copies of all documents given to the military expert. The second issue concerns the motion for protective measures for the Witness ZA, which was filed on the 7th of January, 2004. There's a slight correction to be made. In paragraph 9(A) of this motion, the Prosecution is making reference to the fact that the witness was a Bosniak. In fact -- that the witness -- the witness is a Bosniak. In fact, the witness is of Croat ethnicity. This fact, however, doesn't change the motion for protective measures at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So on page 3 of the document mentioned, paragraph 9(A), "the witness is a Bosniak" should be replaced by the words: "the witness is a Croat"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Very well. So having stated this matter for the sake of our work, we're going to call the first witness in. And I would like to ask the usher to call the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you have already testified at a previous hearing, we won't ask you to spell your name or to take the solemn declaration. So you will just continue with your testimony. So let us start with the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, on the 10th of December last year, before the winter break, you informed the Trial Chamber, amongst other things, about details of the attack on Miletici on the 24th of April, 1993, the treatment you and the other villagers received during and after the attack from the attacking troops, and you also informed the Trial Chamber of the selection of Franjo, Tihomir, and your brother, Vlado Pavlovic, to kneel down. You also identified the houses of Stipo, Srecko and Ivo Pavlovic. Mrs. Kovacevic, today I wanted to continue where we had to discontinue on the 10th of December last year. Prior to finishing your testimony on the 10th of December, you said that you and other villagers, with the exception of Franjo, Tihomir, and your brother, Vlado Pavlovic, you were lined up two by two to go to Mehurici. The question is: Did you actually go to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We went to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How far is Mehurici from Miletici, roughly?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know exactly in metres or kilometres, but it's not that close. I don't know, but it's not close by. It takes more than half an hour on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Did you go voluntarily to Mehurici, you and the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They tied our hands, and they lined us up in a column, two by two, and they took us there. No one asked us whether we wanted to go or not. They just lined us up and took us to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who are you referring to when you say "they lined us up"?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Muslim army, those people who had come to attack our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did ABiH soldiers escort you whilst you were walking to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them went with us; others stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Mr. President, in answer to the Prosecutor's question, the witness answered that -- "did it apply to the Muslim army that took us there." However, later on in the question the Prosecutor used words that the witness didn't use. So that is our objection. So could the wording of the question be changed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, if my recollection isn't wrong, the witness on the 10th of December identified the Muslim army, the army she's referring to today, as the ABiH; however, I'm prepared to change the language of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, I'll repeat the question. Did the Muslim soldiers escort you whilst you were walking to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some men went with us in uniform. We were under shock, and we couldn't really turn around, but in any case they did escort us down there as far as Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did soldiers from the attacking army stay behind in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Some did stay behind in Miletici. Some went with us; some stayed behind. We couldn't turn around and look.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The soldiers who stayed behind, did they stay behind with Franjo Pavlovic, Tihomir Pavlovic, and your brother, Vlado Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just turned around and saw my brother and these three men on their knees. Some of them stayed behind. I didn't look around. I just looked at my brother. I saw them kneeling, and then I continued along my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: A different issue, Mrs. Kovacevic: Franjo Pavlovic, did Franjo Pavlovic have a car?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had a Fico, a small Fiat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to this car on the 24th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The car was taken away while we were up there. It was taken away, and I don't know anything more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you know who took it away? I'm not referring to the name, but do you have any idea who took it away?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I know that a gentleman came and he asked Franjo, "Whose car is this?" And he said, "It's mine," and he brought his keys and he took it away, he drove it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The gentleman you are referring to, Mrs. Kovacevic, has he been a Muslim soldier?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any insignia on him. I can't remember. I don't know whether he was a soldier or not. I don't know. I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In Mehurici, Mrs. Kovacevic, what happened to you after you arrived in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Mehurici, they took us to a house. The women were put up separately, and the men were separated from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After the separation, what happened to you and the other women?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that house, we women were there and we waited to see what would happen to us. We knew nothing about our men. And then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes. And then ...?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we waited there, and then Ribo Suljo came, and he negotiated with them that they release us and he negotiated. And then a bus came to fetch us, and they took us up there to a village called Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After the 24th of April, 1993, when you had to leave Miletici, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you came back to Miletici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We returned to Miletici, but I don't know whether it was a Sunday or a Monday, but we did go back there. And when we arrived, we saw our dead, and then UNPROFOR arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you here, Mrs. Kovacevic. You're not sure whether it was a Sunday or a Monday. In terms of a concrete date, was it the next day, the 25th of April, 1993, or the 26th of April, 1993, or a different day?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know the exact day, whether it was a Sunday or a Monday, but no other date. It couldn't have been any other date. I'm just not sure whether it was Sunday or Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What day was it when the attack was executed on the 24th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Sunday or the Monday you are referring to, is it the Sunday or the Monday following the Saturday of the attack?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were down there at Luka, and then we went up there. I don't know whether we spent the night at Luka. And we went to the village. But whether it was a Sunday or a Monday, I really can't remember. It was one of those two days. I just don't know. But we did go to the village, myself, my mother, father, sister, and some other villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Mrs. Kovacevic, there was no week between the day of the attack and the day you went back to Miletici? Was it either the next day or the day after?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the next day. When we were taken to Mehurici, it was Saturday. Then we were in Luka. And then the next day, Sunday. But I am not sure. I don't know whether it was the next day or the day after, the Monday. I can't remember exactly. But I think it was Sunday that we went back to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Prior to you going back, Mrs. Kovacevic, had you received any information in between, meaning after you had left and prior to coming back?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR told us at Luka. We asked, "What happened to our people in the village?" And they said that they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When you came back to Miletici, either on the 25th or the 26th of April, 1993, were there still Muslim soldiers in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came from Luka to the village, there was one Muslim soldier at the entrance to the village as we came, and then several came to the village but we were still in a state of shock and we saw our dead there. But at first I did see one of them at the entrance to the village, as we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The first soldier you've seen and the other ones you've seen in Miletici at the day of your return, were these local Muslim soldiers or foreign Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to tell you that, whether they were local or foreign. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did these soldiers look like the Mujahedin you were describing in your testimony on the 10th of December last year?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They didn't look like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What did you do once you went back to Miletici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came to Miletici, we first went to the house where our dead were. And then we went to our own house. We spent most of the time in the centre of the village. We were standing around and waiting to see what would happen to us. We didn't do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You first went to the house where your dead were. Which house was it, Mrs. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Ivo Pavlovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can I please ask the registrar to recall the Exhibit P22 and to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, can you please tell the Trial Chamber whether this photograph shows the house of Ivo Pavlovic you were just referring to? The photograph will within a few moments also appear on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Inside this house on this photograph of Ivo Pavlovic, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inside I saw our dead in the room on the ground floor, and they were covered with blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whom are you referring to when you are saying "our dead"?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to Tihomir Pavlovic, Vlado Pavlovic, Franjo Pavlovic. I didn't look any more. I just looked at my brother. I saw him and Tihomir, and I didn't dare look on, because they were closest to the window. They were the first I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How far away have been the bodies of Tihomir Pavlovic, Vlado Pavlovic, and Franjo Pavlovic when you had a look from the window?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe 2 or 3 metres from the window. I can't tell you exactly. I just saw them through this window.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether the faces of the bodies of the dead you were just referring to could be seen.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Tihomir and Vlado's faces, and I didn't see others, but I did see the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, I'm now going to show you a number of photographs and I wish you to tell the Trial Chamber whether you can identify the individuals shown on these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, these photographs have already been tendered into evidence under seal in the course of the testimony of a witness who testified in closed session. I will therefore tender again into evidence the very same photographs. I have been advised by the registrar that in such a situation the photographs should be tendered under the same exhibit number; however, with a .1 at the end. With your permission I'm now going to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please remind the Chamber and the Defence and the accused what was the exhibit number of these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we actually have the photographs with us. We can show you -- we can show the photographs via Sanction. And we also have hard copies of the very same photographs with us. And the exhibit numbers were P23 through P27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So they were admitted under Exhibit Numbers P23 to 27. So the Prosecution is now going to show these photographs, P23 to 27, to the witness. So the photographs that are going to be shown to the witness will retain the same exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I actually would like to show the witness first the photograph Exhibit Number P27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have five photographs. So the usher is going to place under the ELMO P27. The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the photographs are shown, the Defence doesn't really see what the purpose of the Prosecutor is in showing these photographs to the witness, though we are not objecting to this particular fact. These photographs have already been identified and admitted into evidence. Secondly, the photographs were made seven days after the event, and the witness said that she saw the faces of her brother. Thirdly, this is the witness's brother, and I really don't see that it is necessary to upset the witness once again by showing her these photographs. And those are the reasons why we feel that it is unnecessary to show these exhibits again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But as the Defence knows, it is up to the Prosecution to prove the facts. The burden of proof is with the Prosecution. And on the one hand, the witness needs to formally identify her brother as well as the other victims. I think that was the intention of the Prosecution, to confirm through this witness the accuracy of the identification of the victims, including her brother. Therefore, P27. The usher is going to show the witness photograph P27. Should the usher have the photograph in his hands? So we have P27 on the screen now. Put your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, can you please tell the Trial Chamber the body of whom you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph, I see the body of Vito Pavlovic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown the Exhibit Number P24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the photograph shown to her, could she identify in handwriting the name of the person. Could she write it down. Because in the transcript she says that she saw the body of Vito Pavlovic. So she should mark that down. Madam Witness, will you please write down on the photograph that this is a photograph of Vito Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said I saw the body of Mr. Stipo Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Because on the transcript it said "Vito," so that's an error in the transcript. So it's Stipo Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please also put down today's date, 12th of January, 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher is going to show the document now to the Defence and the accused. So my conclusion is that the Prosecution wishes to tender this document as identified by this witness, but the exhibit number will remain the same, that is, P27. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest to call it P27.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit number will be P27.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness now, please, be shown the photograph or the exhibit P24.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, can you please inform the Trial Chamber whom you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph, I see the body of Tihomir Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Witness, will you please write down on that photograph the name of Tihomir Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And also today's date, the 12th of January, 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher will now show this document to Defence counsel, as well as to the accused. Mr. Registrar, will you give me the exhibit number now, please. I suppose P24.1?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is P24.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown the very same exhibit once again, P24.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Usher, pick up the document again, please, and show it once again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, you just have said that you have seen the face of Tihomir Pavlovic. On the photograph in front of you, you will see a wound in the face of the person you identified as Tihomir Pavlovic. The day you went back to Miletici, did Tihomir Pavlovic have the very same wound in his face?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that through the window. I saw this other side. But I heard from our people - and others can confirm it - that Tihomir Pavlovic did have this wound on his face. But I didn't see it with my own eyes; others did, and they spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness now, please, be shown the photograph, Exhibit P25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But before we do so, could the usher give Mr. Registrar document P24.1. So we will now show the witness document P25.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, can you inform the Trial Chamber whose body you can see on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the body of Franjo Pavlovic in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please date and sign it once again for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the name of the person that you have identified, that you have recognised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document will be shown to the Defence now. To the accused. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is P25.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the witness now, please, be shown Exhibit P26, ERN 02032398.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, can you please again identify the body on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the body of Ante Petrovic in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please again date and sign it and write the name of the body on the bottom of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher will show the Defence this exhibit. And the accused. And, Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number is P26.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can the witness please be shown the exhibit, photograph P23.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, we know that this is a very difficult situation for you, but can you please identify the person which is shown on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in this photograph is Vlado Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mrs. Kovacevic, that you've seen the face of your brother, Vlado Pavlovic, on the 24th of April.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the face of Vlado Pavlovic from the window. But it was at some distance. I didn't see the face clearly. I only saw it from the window, and then I left. I didn't look at it any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, given that she has mentioned the name and the date, could you show this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is P23.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How far away have you been when you have seen the face of your brother, Vlado, and for how long have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw my brother from the window of the house. I only had a look through the window. I didn't go in there at all. A minute ago I said what the distance was, 2 or 3 metres. I don't know exactly. But all I can say is that I saw him through the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, could we now return to the first photograph of the house. Because I'm under the impression that there are a number of windows, and a window has been mentioned but the Trial Chamber would like to know which window is being referred to exactly, since the building consists of a number of floors and it would be useful to pinpoint the exact window. Witness, on the basis of the photograph of the house, would you be able to tell us which window is concerned exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's this window here, this one, behind this column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, when you saw the victim through the window, you were standing then between -- at the site between the two poles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. I was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. standing between the two poles by the window here. Yes. I saw him through the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Everyone has noted that there are two poles, and the witness told us that she was between the two poles. There is a window between the poles, and it is from this position that she saw the body. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the matter is a lot clearer now. Mr. Withopf, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long have you seen the face of your brother, Vlado?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw him through that window, and then I turned to where my mother and sister were. I didn't look at him for long, because I wasn't able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: All right. Moving on to a different issue, Mrs. Kovacevic, and it won't take long from my side any more. After you went back to Miletici on the 25th or the 26th of April, 1993, were the houses in Miletici still intact?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They had broken into the houses, and my house had been broken into. The door had been broken down. We entered the house, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: But ...? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went into the house, my mother, my sister, and myself. My father was there too. And as UNPROFOR told us that we wouldn't be staying there, we went in to take some things that we needed. We took some photographs and some clothes and we returned to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just informing the Trial Chamber that your house had been broken into. What was the situation in respect to the other houses in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't look around, but I heard from other local villagers that they had broken into the houses. But I didn't go from house to house, because we were still in a state of fear. I entered my house, I collected some of my affairs and returned to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When did you then finally leave Miletici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left on that day. As I said a minute ago, I don't remember exactly whether it was on the 25th or the 26th, but we left with UNPROFOR on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Since then, did you ever go back to Miletici?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never went back to Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the time being I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf, your examination-in-chief for this witness has therefore been completed? Have I understood this well?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's the correct understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now proceed with the cross-examination, but we will have a break first of all, to allow the witness to rest. And, Witness, after the break - which will last for 25 minutes - the Defence for the accused who are here will cross-examine you. And if necessary, the Prosecution may ask you some questions again. But before we suspend the session, before we adjourn, the Trial Chamber has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you left with UNPROFOR. When you looked at the victims through the window, was UNPROFOR present at that time?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. UNPROFOR wasn't there when we arrived and when I first saw those bodies. UNPROFOR wasn't present at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how long after did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember after how much time UNPROFOR arrived. I don't know exactly. All I know is that we were in the village for some time before they arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is half past 3.00. We'll have a 25-minute break, and we will continue at five to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll continue. But the witness must be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mrs. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic and I represent the general, Enver Hadzihasanovic. I'll put a certain number of questions to you, and please answer if you can. I would just like to ask you to make a brief pause after my question, wait for the English interpretation to finish, and then you can answer my question, so that everyone present in the courtroom - and the Trial Chamber in particular - may be in a position to follow our conversation. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it correct, Mrs. Kovacevic, to say that your village is in the municipality of Travnik and was in the municipality of Travnik before? Witness, have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness -- witness, have you heard the question put to you by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood the question, but I wasn't sure whether I had to answer the question immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is your village located in the municipality of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that the village of Miletici consists of Gornji and Donji Miletici, two hamlets?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that before the war there were about 40 Croats, 40 inhabitants in the village, and there were between 25 and 30 in April 1993? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the time of the attack against the village there were between 25 to 30 of them. But before the attack, to be quite frank, I don't know how many inhabitants there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that in the other hamlet there were four families named Suljic, Brace [phoen], Avdo, Dedo and Akif? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that both hamlets were in a mountainous region, on the slopes of Vlasic Mountain?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to answer that question. I know that the lower village of Miletici, where these brothers lived, was below our village, but I don't know. I know they were below our village and we were up in the hill, a little further up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mount Vlasic is above your village; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Above our village -- Mount Vlasic is on the other side of our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's not important. In December, in response to a question put to you by the Prosecution, you said that up until that time your relations with your Muslim neighbours were exceptionally good; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. We didn't have any problems until that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you will agree with me if I say that as early as March, and especially after the massacre in Ahmici, guards were set up in the village. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People went on guard duty in the village, but I don't know what you mean, whether it was on that account. But people did go on guard duty in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, in addition to that, your good relations with your neighbours -- in spite of that, your relations with your neighbours from Donji Miletici did not deteriorate; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did not deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are aware of the fact that the Suljic brothers were members of the BH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were members of the BH army. I couldn't say. But all I know is that they came up to our village. But I can't answer that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But men fit for military service from your village were HVO members and they were part of the Frankopan Brigade, whose command was located in Guca Gora; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, I couldn't say. I know that my brother didn't go anywhere. He didn't go to any battlefields. I know that he went on guard duty in the village, but he didn't go to any battlefields.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a Prosecution question in December, you said that on the 24th of April Pero Suljic came to the village to warn you about the threat posed by the Mujahedin, who had been seen in the vicinity of the village; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When he told you that according to his information the Mujahedin had gone to the nearby village of Skradno, which is about an hour on foot from your village, and he said he hoped that they wouldn't attack the village; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that the Mujahedin had gone to the Skomorje village, not the Skradno village but the Skomorje village. And he said that if anything happened to us, they would protect us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you spoke about whether the Mujahedin might come or not, one of the Suljic brothers, together with Franjo Pavlovic, went to inform the command in the village of Mehurici of the possibility of the Mujahedin arriving; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be frank, I don't know. I was in the village, but we were in a state of panic and I really don't know. I don't know whether he went down there with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that soon after their arrival there was shooting around the village, and you took shelter in Stipo Pavlovic's house. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Stipo Pavlovic was the only person to return fire from his house.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the attackers threw a grenade -- they then threw a grenade and Stipo died and his wife, Lucija was wounded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were leaving the house, you saw that one of the attackers had also been killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You then saw that there were foreigners, called Mujahedin, among the attackers and they were speaking a foreign language and they had beards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There were some local Muslims with them too, and you knew that they had join the Mujahedin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The local Muslims wore ski masks or they had camouflage paint on their faces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether they had these ski masks, but they had camouflage paint on. As far as their faces are concerned, yes, that's correct. But I didn't pay that much attention to it, since I was in a state of shock.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from these faces that had camouflage paint on them, you didn't notice any other insignia on them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the attacker who was killed, he was also camouflaged. But you recognised one of the young men who had joined -- one of the local young men who had joined the Mujahedin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that attacker was wearing camouflage paint. We left the house and we passed by him. That was in the middle of the village. But I don't know if you can understand this, but we were in a state of shock and -- well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I really won't insist on you telling us anything that you can't remember for sure. However, on that day, the brothers Suljic, Dedo, Akif and Avdo who were with you, they were wearing civilian clothes and they weren't carrying arms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't think they were armed, but I do think that they were in civilian clothes. But to tell you the truth, I can't really remember how they were dressed. I don't think they were in uniform. They were in -- they were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At one point one of the Mujahedin hit one of the inhabitants of your village, a Croat, and Akif Suljic intervened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that point the Mujahedin hit Akif Suljic in the head with the butt of his rifle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I don't know that person who hit him, but I know that he did hit him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And made him bleed?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Prosecution, both in December and today, you said that your hands had been tied up and that they took you in the direction of Mehurici. At the same time, Dedo and Akif Suljic were taken in the direction of Mehurici and their hands had been tied up too. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think I said that they had been tied up. I can't remember exactly whether I said that, but I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is my question now. But they were taken to Mehurici with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't even remember that detail. I can't remember whether they were taken there with us. It's difficult for me to remember everything. That happened some time ago. I think you can understand me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. And I'm sorry to have to distress you again, but it's my duty to ask you to answer the questions, if you know the answers. While you were still in the village, can you remember or do you know whether they called one of the Mujahedin Ramadan?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Mehurici, you were taken to a house where Serbs used to live before and which was also under the control of the Mujahedin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Mujahedin controlled them, but yes, we were taken to that house. Who controlled it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is where they separated the men from the women, as you said, and it was only several hours later, about midnight, that you were released.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were released - I think you can answer this question, and I hope you will - were at the same time two Serbs released and a Muslim who had also been detained in these houses by the Mujahedin? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know anything about that. To be quite frank, I don't know about those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned colleague just put in the question that the house was guarded by Mujahedin. The witness has answered the question to the contrary, that she does not know whether the house was guarded by Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you rephrase the question, please, regarding who was guarding the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there's no need for me to ask that question again, because the witness said she didn't know, which means that she cannot say who was guarding it. So to repeat the question I think would be superfluous. I don't wish to bother the witness by tiring her with -- by insisting on questions she cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To satisfy everyone, let me ask the witness. Madam Witness, and for the benefit of the Judges, to the best of your knowledge did you know who was guarding the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who held that house. We were brought there during the night. We were inside. And I said a moment ago - and I'm saying again - I don't know who held that house, who controlled it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were released, you saw Ribo Suljo, your pre-war teacher of geography in the elementary school in Mehurici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ribo Suljo was wearing the uniform of the army and he was a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know whether he was in uniform and whether he was a member, but he did negotiate with them our release.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was precisely my next question. Ribo Suljo was one of the people who negotiated with the Mujahedin that they release you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ribo Suljo and other members of the army ensured a bus with which they transported you to the village of Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, Ribo Suljo and others wanted to provide better shelter for you elsewhere, and he put you up in a house next to his, the house of his grandparents in the village of Luka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That night you were guarded by members of the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KATICA KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who guarded us. I know that we were in that house. Now, who was outside and who guarded us, I don't know. I just know that we were in that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kovacevic, I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do Defence counsel for Mr. Kubura have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence for Mr. Kubura has no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Has the Prosecution any additional questions, in view of the questions put by the Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Witness, you came to The Hague at the request of the Prosecution. You have answered questions from the Prosecution, as well as from the Defence. The Chamber noted these questions revived painful memories for you, and we fully appreciate that the questions caused you some suffering and this was trying for you, but it was necessary for you to come and testify in this case. The Chamber thanks you for coming, and we wish you a safe journey home since you already came in December. We would like to ask the usher to accompany you out and we would like to convey to you our condolences once again for your family loss. Mr. Usher, please accompany the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue with the next witness, I should like to come back to a small procedural issue. We noted a moment ago that the Prosecution produced photographs which had already been admitted into evidence. We found that the procedure took some time because it was necessary to authenticate the identity of the persons on those photographs, to have the photographs initialled, to show those photographs to the Defence and the accused, and all this takes time, especially if we have to do it again with other witnesses. So if the Defence is agreeable, we could proceed in the following manner: Using the computerised system, the witness can look at the screen, authenticate the photograph on the screen, and then the transcript would register this authentication by the witness. This procedure would, of course, apply for witnesses of the Prosecution as well as for witnesses of the Defence, when their turn comes and when they call witnesses. And in this way, we will all save some time. Since the photographs had already been admitted, the number remains the same and there's no need to give it a new exhibit number. Is there any objection on the part of the Defence against this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the beginning we drew attention to this fact. Exhibits that have already been admitted into evidence probably need not to be re-admitted. Secondly, the fact of death was admitted by the Defence before the beginning of the proceedings, so there's no need to reconfirm certain facts again during the hearing itself. Thirdly, if we have such a procedure that you are suggesting, then the Defence can immediately say that we can confirm that the witness will identify those persons. In order to economise, there's no need to waste time by showing them again. But I do believe that we all have to bear in mind the emotions of the witness, who is certainly upset by this whole procedure. And for this reason, the Defence fully agrees with your suggestion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is much in favour of such a procedure; however, the statement just made by my learned colleague is not completely correct. It's not about identification only; it's also about the witness given a chance and giving a description of certain wounds on the bodies of the victims. The Defence has only stipulated to the fact that the persons named in the indictment are dead, and to nothing else. The Prosecution case goes beyond that, and it is at least an issue for sentencing at a later stage of these proceedings. Therefore, these photographs have to be shown to the witnesses, but they can be shown in the manner just -- as just said by you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, that is how we will proceed. I just wish to specify that we had a situation a moment ago which could repeat itself, that the witness was shocked by seeing these photographs. And if such witnesses need any psychological support, we should plan for it following the hearing. So this is a fact that we all have to bear in mind, because we see that some witnesses, at least, can be deeply shocked when they are shown exhibits reminding them of the dramas that they lived through. Therefore, we shall continue with the examination of the next witness of the Prosecution. Mr. Usher, will you please bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam. Can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell the Chamber your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Andja Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 2nd of June, 1963.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Cukle, Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a retiree. I'm a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Grubisno Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called by the Prosecution to testify on facts of which the accused have been charged. You need to take a solemn declaration, and will you please read the text in your native language that will be handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Madam, at first the Prosecution, who are seated on your right, will have some questions for you; after that, after those questions put by the Prosecution, the Defence counsel for the accused, who are seated on your left, will have some questions for you; and, if necessary, the Prosecutor have will some additional questions after that; and the Judges, who are in front of you, if they so wish, may also ask you questions at any point in time. And therefore, it is under these conditions that your testimony will take place. Without wasting any more time, I would like to ask the Prosecution to start with the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Have you ever been married?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date you were married and to whom you were married.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date when I was officially married. It was on the 25th of December, 1992 [as interpreted], and I married Franjo Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, upon being married to Franjo Pavlovic, where did you reside?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For how long did you reside in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: For ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there's an error in the transcript. I think the witness said that she married in 1982, and here it says 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, when did you get married, in 1982 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, when the war broke out in Bosnia, you were living in Miletici at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber the events leading up to the commencement of the war in Bosnia as it related to your life in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let's start with the situation prior to the war. Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber the ethnic composition of the village of Miletici.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in the area inhabited by Croats, and a little further away, about a kilometre and a half away, were the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the area where the Muslims lived have a name?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Miletici. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you please tell us briefly about the state of relations between the Croats and the Muslims in Miletici prior to the commencement of the war.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Relations were good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Witness, when those relations changed?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Not until they attacked Miletici. But until then, everything was fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prior to the attack on Miletici, did you notice anything unusual in the area around Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I went to Cukle, in Jezerce, when I went to see my family, I saw some Mujahedin sitting in front of a house. And if I went to Travnik, I would see them near the school in Mehurici, the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us what you mean by "Mujahedin." What does that term mean to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The Mujahedin, foreign soldiers, foreign Muslim soldiers who had come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you know these people were foreign Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: They had a different accent. They spoke differently. And their appearance differed from our Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please clarify what you mean by "their appearance differed." How so?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: They were darker. They were much darker. Their faces, the colour of their skin was much darker than that of our Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the first time you saw any of these Mujahedin? You've told us where, but do you recall the approximate month or year when you first saw these people?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to focus your attention now on the spring of 1993, Witness. At that time, were you still living in Miletici with your husband, Franjo Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have anyone else living with you, any other family members residing with you in your house at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. My husband's brother, my husband's mother and sister, and my children with were us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Witness, when your children were relocated elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber where your children went and approximately when they went there.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: We took the children a week before that to Cukle to stay with my husband's sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "a week before that," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: About seven days earlier, I took them to my husband's sisters at Cukle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me try to clarify my question. You say "seven days earlier." Seven days earlier than what?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Before the attack on Miletici, when they killed our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of the attack on Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: The 24th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it was seven days prior to the 24th of April, 1993 that your children were taken to Cukle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like you to focus your attention on the 24th of April, 1993. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber where you were on the morning of that day and what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I was at home. It was a Saturday. I was cleaning the house, as I always do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know where your husband was on the morning of the 24th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: My husband went to plough the fields. It was the planting season.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was he ploughing the fields owned by your husband and yourself, or was he ploughing someone else's fields?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: He was ploughing for our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the name of the neighbours whose fields your husband was ploughing on the 24th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Mande [phoen] Pavlovic's fields and Sreco Pavlovic. And he was finishing off at Sreco Pavlovic's fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your husband, once he was finishing ploughing or helping the neighbours plough their fields, where did your husband go?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: He came home to have a bath, and then he would go back to Sreco's for dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time he came home to have a bath that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It was about ten to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that he was -- he would then go back to Sreco's for dinner. Why was he going to Sreco's for dinner?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Because it is customary when you're helping somebody in the fields, then you have dinner at his place at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your husband in fact go to Sreco's house for dinner on the 24th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because he returned home to have a bath and we went to have coffee. And when he had a look through the window, he saw that something strange was happening outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the strange thing that was happening outside was?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: When he had a look through the window, he saw Ana Petrovic crying and he saw Dedo Suljic behind Ivo Pavlovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber where he saw these individuals. Where were they in the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: In front of Ivo Pavlovic's house. And Ana Petrovic was behind Ivo Pavlovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask that the witness be shown a photograph. This is a photograph I would ask the witness to make some markings on, so it's not one that we have at this point electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This photograph has never been tendered into evidence then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I stand corrected. We do have an electronic copy, and a previous witness identified certain features on this photograph. However, we would ask this witness to make a number of markings on the photograph, and so I think perhaps in this case it might be better to have a fresh copy of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would ask that that be placed on the ELMO, please, and that the witness be provided with a fine-tip marker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently we don't have a pen for the witness.
